title: Thought Experiment: How Could One Save Nauru?
summary:
Nauru (now officially Naoero), an island nation in the pacific and the third smallest country in the world, once one of the wealthiest, is now 80% uninhabitable after intensive phosphate mining devastated the landscape.

It’s sovereign wealth fund was badly mismanaged during it’s heyday, and despite efforts to make it economically viable as a tax haven, or geopolitically useful as a location for offshore asylum processing, it probably doesn’t have many decades before it becomes completely impossible to survive there. Not least because the majority of the country’s 12,000 strong population is confined to a narrow habitable strip of the island, which is slowly being eaten away by the sea.

So my question is, if you had infinite financial resources, and there were no geopolitical or diplomatic hurdles, and you’d decided to try and save Nauru (which we can say would mean making it both habitable and able to participate again in the global economy in order to sustain itself), how could you do it?

title: Ask HN: Are you prepared to rent intelligence from AI providers?
summary:
Say the year 2035 arrives, and for the last ten years you have relied on an AI machine to do your thinking for you because you convinced yourself it made you more productive. As a consequence, your native intelligence has atrophied, and you now depend on this synthetic pseudo-brain the way a diabetic depends on insulin after the pancreas has failed.

Then AI providers put a tollbooth on thinking. What happens if you can't afford to rent your thinking? You are left with the intelligence of a farm animal, because your natural brain has become useless.

title: Open-Source FPGA The "startup idea" to "go big fast"
summary:
FPGAs are general purpose and can be made to do anything. They are basically a function of the number of repeated elements. They are "commodity items" except for one fact.

The current FPGA manufacturers won't disclose the details of the design internals to "protect their intellectual property".

Only small FPGAs have been reverse engineered and there are some high-quality tools that have been developed. Their limitation is information.

Because of high costs set by the big players the ability to build truly complex FPGA designs (e.g. an NVIDIA competitor or an ARM competitor or a high-function inference chip) is "closed source information" limited.

But by design FPGAs are basicaly simple repeated elements that can be scaled to any size. That means that a new open sourced chip could be a range from really tiny to enormous with cost purely a function of chip die area. This makes it a pure commodity play.

Some "bright spot" student wanting to start a company could get funded to create a new FPGA design (e.g. since wires take up most of the area figure out how to put the wires "under the logic" in a multi-layer design). Extend existing open-source software tools chains for the new chip design. Open-source the design and license it which is what made ARM so big.

Within hours I'm certain the FPGA tools would be updated to full support of the new chip, opening the market to real, high powered chips. Or create your own open-source tools. Build the company around selling expertise like consulting on custom board-level designs using the new chips.

Turning highly capable FPGAs into volume chips is a market nobody has addressed. What it needs is someone who wants to be a startup CEO and someone who has capital to create the first design (probably a few million dollars).

Of course if you have access to REAL capital then buy Xilinx or Altera and open source their design and tool chain. The company that doesn't get bought would disappear overnight. (Somebody call Musk with the idea :-) )

If you know someone who wants to "go big fast" either path is a major opportunity.

title: Ask HN: How many of you have replaced your everyday apps with something custom?
summary:
This question isn't specific to vibe-coded apps, I was just curious how many people are using bespoke everyday software, for things like a file explorer, terminal, maybe mail client, text editor etc.

Down the line I had planned on writing my own terminal, text editor and file explorer, but had too many other high priority projects and hadn't gotten around to it yet, and probably wouldn't for another year.

Playing with Claude, after only...six prompts, I have my ideal custom terminal...kitty graphics, iterm style tmux integration, transparency, renaming tabs, session support, other small stuff; it's tailored exactly to my workstyle and aesthetic tastes, and so far is working amazingly.

I see why so much vibe-coded stuff gets released - because it's exciting to share having brought your vision to life. If I had written this pre-AI, I'd be proud of it and want to share, but now, if it only takes six prompts to generate, I'm not sure there would be a point?

title: Tell HN: OpenRouter – "Requests you sent to MiniMax models may have been read"
summary:
Got this email from OpenRouter today:

A security researcher placed unique test URLs in prompts sent to MiniMax models from July to October 2026. A third party accessed those URLs 40 to 130 hours after the requests were sent, whether MiniMax served a request directly or another provider forwarded it to MiniMax. With one exception, the same tests on other models at those providers were not accessed, and none of the AWS test keys were used.

Your account sent 21 requests to MiniMax models through MiniMax, Novita, StreamLake and AtlasCloud, from June 22 at 03:02 to July 3 at 23:28 UTC.

AtlasCloud, Novita and StreamLake have told us they forwarded OpenRouter requests for MiniMax models to MiniMax. Based on what the researcher and these providers have reported, the issue sits with MiniMax and the providers that forwarded to it, not with OpenRouter. We are passing on what they have told us. MiniMax told StreamLake that content moderation was enabled on its endpoints before October 22 and that it has since enabled Zero Data Retention. We have asked MiniMax for its own account and have not received one.

This means a third party may have read the prompts and outputs of these requests. While we investigate, we have removed the Zero Data Retention label from these MiniMax-model endpoints.

Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50591694
